extracted.intended_audience: Reviewers assigned to CVPR 2026 (program committee / area reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and criteria for how CVPR 2026 reviewers should evaluate papers, write reviews, handle rebuttals, and act ethically and responsibly during the review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core principles: fairness, thoughtfulness, consistency, transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: We want to make the best decisions we can to serve the community. Our goal is to be fair, thoughtful, and consistent. We also want our decisions to be transparent—even if an author isn't happy with the outcome, they should be able to see clearly why that decision was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep policies clear and understood to minimize confusion, frustration, and appeals. Use these principles to guide tone, thoroughness, and clarity of reasoning in reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer role: provide recommendations, not decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Your job is to make well-reasoned recommendations that help Area Chairs (ACs) decide which papers should be accepted to CVPR. You provide recommendations, not decisions—the final acceptance decisions are made by ACs, Senior Area Chairs, and Program Chairs based on your input and the full context of submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on clear evidence and reasoning to enable ACs to synthesize opinions; explain the basis of your recommendation rather than issuing a verdict without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual purpose of reviews: inform decisions and help authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Your review serves two purposes: it helps decision-makers understand the paper's merits and weaknesses, and it provides constructive feedback to help authors improve their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write reviews that both justify your recommendation for the AC and give actionable suggestions to authors for improvement (regardless of acceptance outcome).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support opinions with evidence and explain reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Support your opinions with evidence, and avoid making up your own policies. Write reviews that clearly explain your reasoning and respond to rebuttals fairly and on time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite specific parts of the paper or prior work when claiming 'done before' or when critiquing correctness; avoid blank assertions and subjective one-liners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain professional objectivity and respectful tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain professional objectivity—focus on the work itself, not your assumptions about the authors. Treat everyone involved with fairness, compassion, and consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep tone professional, avoid second-person address (avoid "you" or "the authors" in accusatory ways), avoid sarcasm or dismissive language; ensure review is constructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and confidentiality obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect anonymity, confidentiality, and the intellectual content of submissions. Do not share, reuse, or build on ideas from submissions. Destroy materials after the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect double-blind review (avoid author-identity searches), declare and avoid conflicts of interest promptly, handle human subjects and personal data with heightened scrutiny, and never discuss submissions outside the review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict-of-interest and reporting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare and avoid conflicts of interest promptly. If you notice any improprieties, report them through the proper channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you suspect policy violations (plagiarism, dual submission, fabricated results, unethical data use, prompt injection, human-subjects violations, etc.) alert your AC immediately and do not investigate independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: What should be accepted: soundness, contribution, and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend acceptance for papers that will interest CVPR attendees, are technically sound, and contribute meaningfully (methodologically, empirically, or conceptually). Balance novelty with significance and potential impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor fixable issues should not drive rejection. Be cautious with scope judgments—CVPR values breadth. Consider reproducibility, data contribution, ethical data use, societal impact, and limitations discussions positively. A paper doesn't need to be perfect to be accepted—it needs to advance the field and meet quality standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible Reviewing Policy and timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: CVPR 2026 strictly enforces the Responsible Reviewing Policy and Reviewing Deadline Policy. Irresponsible reviews include short or generic text not tied to the paper's specifics, factual errors suggesting superficial reading, and content generated or substantially assisted by LLMs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: Irresponsible or late reviews may trigger desk rejection of all papers on which the reviewer is an author. Allocate time and give each paper appropriate effort; follow deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM usage policy for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: LLMs must not be used to generate, translate, paraphrase, or otherwise compose review content. Sharing any part of any submission (the paper, quotes from the paper, captions, figures, etc.) with LLMs is strictly prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted uses: non-confidential background research on publicly available concepts or methods (not the submission itself); grammar checks of short phrases you have already written (under ~50 words, containing no submission-specific content). Prohibited uses: inputting any text, figures, or content from the submission into an LLM; using LLMs to summarize, paraphrase, or analyze the paper; using LLMs to draft any portion of your review; using LLMs to translate the paper or your review. Enforcement: violations may lead to a two-year ban and should be reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review workflow — Step 1: preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspect your stack promptly for conflicts and suitability. Review your stack holistically and plan your time wisely. Allocate effort based on each paper’s complexity and scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inform your AC immediately if reassignment is needed. Review relevant policies and guidelines. If you suspect a policy violation, alert the Chairs but review as if no violation occurred (they will investigate separately).

rubrics_metrics.name: Review workflow — Step 2: careful reading and brief summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the paper thoroughly, taking notes as you go. Draft a short, accurate summary in your own words (2-4 sentences). This summary helps reveal gaps in your understanding—if you can't summarize it clearly, read again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess correctness, completeness, clarity of contribution, and positioning versus prior work. Identify the paper's core claims and evaluate the evidence supporting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review workflow — Step 3: writing the review (required content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Your review should include: a concise summary (2-4 sentences covering what the paper does and claims); strengths (specific, evidence-based points); weaknesses (specific, evidence-based concerns); constructive suggestions (how authors could address weaknesses); and a justified recommendation (clearly connecting your assessment to your rating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Back 'done before' claims with specific references and explain relationships to prior work. Do not over-weight SOTA tables alone—consider experimental design, insights, and broader contributions. Keep tone professional; avoid second-person address; be specific and concrete; avoid vague statements like 'the paper is interesting'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review workflow — Step 3: check for standard errors and biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Check your review for standard errors: ignorance and inaccuracy, pure opinion, novelty fallacy, blank assertions, policy entrepreneurism, and intellectual laziness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and better practices are provided (e.g., if you claim a theorem is false, provide specific evidence; if you say 'this has been done before' cite references and explain differences). Avoid equating novelty with quality or inventing requirements not in policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review workflow — Step 4: rebuttal and discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the rebuttal carefully and engage substantively. Update your ratings and review if the rebuttal addresses your concerns. Explain what changed your mind and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not demand substantial new experiments in rebuttal; small, reasonable checks are acceptable. Focus on clarifications and addressing misunderstandings rather than requesting new work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review workflow — Step 5: finalization and final justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Participate in AC-reviewer discussions. Ensure your reasoning is clear to the AC. Submit your final rating and well-justified final recommendation by the deadline. Your final justification should be specific, evidence-based, and clearly connected to your rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unacceptable final justifications include vague or contradictory statements (examples given). Good final justification examples illustrate tying evidence, novelty, experiments, and rebuttal outcomes to the final rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working with your Area Chair (responsibilities and expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a clear, well-reasoned recommendation; explain the evidence and reasoning behind your assessment; read rebuttals carefully and update your review if warranted; participate actively in discussions during the decision phase; ensure prompt responses to AC questions; flag any concerns about policy violations or ethical issues immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect AC support resolving conflicts, guidance on policy questions, coordination with SACs/PCs on serious issues, and assistance if the paper is outside your expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common reviewing pitfalls (error types to avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common errors include: Ignorance / Inaccuracy, Pure Opinion, Novelty Fallacy, Blank Assertions, Policy Entrepreneurism, and Intellectual Laziness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each error type the guideline provides a 'bad practice' example and a 'better practice' alternative (e.g., replace blanket claims with specific counterexamples or citations; don't demand beating SOTA on all benchmarks; don't invent extra requirements like mandatory code release). Use the provided better practices when composing critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final review checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Before submitting your review, verify: brief, accurate paper summary present; paper checked for standard errors (incorrect mathematics, omitted material such as experiments/context/citations); 'done before' claims supported; strengths and weaknesses stated with specific evidence; review is not too short; tone is professional and constructive; review checked for standard mistakes; policy compliance (LLM use, confidentiality, conflicts) checked; submitted before the deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist as a final gate to ensure your review is actionable, justified, and policy-compliant.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to escalate / report concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediately alert your AC if you suspect: plagiarism or self-plagiarism; dual submission to multiple venues; unethical data use or privacy violations; fabricated results or falsified experiments; violation of withdrawn-dataset norms; prompt injection or LLM abuse; violations of human subjects research protocols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not investigate independently. Report concerns and let the appropriate committees handle the investigation; continue reviewing the paper as usual unless instructed otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dos and Don'ts summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick actionable dos and don'ts: DO ground judgments in evidence and citations; be specific and constructive; engage substantively with rebuttals; flag conflicts of interest immediately; respect confidentiality and anonymity; meet all deadlines. DON'T use LLMs to generate or analyze review content; don't share submission content; don't search for author identities; don't invent policy requirements; don't make unsupported assertions; don't submit generic or superficial reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this as a short behavioural checklist to guide everyday review practices and avoid the most common policy and quality failures.
